blocks.content: Delhi's geography chapter is unusually layered for exam purposes: beyond basic physical facts, questions frequently test its unique triple identity — a city, a Union Territory, and (since 1991) a special 'National Capital Territory' — plus its position within the still-larger National Capital Region (NCR). Keep this three-tier terminology (city / UT / NCT) straight, as it is a recurring source of exam confusion.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Delhi is geographically situated in Northern India, bordered by Haryana on three sides and Uttar Pradesh to the east.
The Delhi Ridge is the northernmost structural extension of the ancient Aravalli Mountain Range.
The River Yamuna forms the natural eastern boundary of the Delhi region.
The regional climate is characterized by extreme continental conditions with distinct hot summers and cold winters.

blocks.content: Delhi lies in north India on the west bank of the Yamuna River, at the point where the Indo-Gangetic Plain meets a low outlying spur of the Aravalli Range — the Delhi Ridge — giving the city a distinctive mix of flat riverine plain and low rocky hills.

The National Capital Territory of Delhi is landlocked and bordered by only two states: Haryana on the west, north and south, and Uttar Pradesh on the east (across the Yamuna) — a compact, two-state border pattern similar in structure (though not scale) to Chandigarh's two-state framing.
Delhi is one of the smallest states/UTs of India by area yet, owing to its status as national capital and a major metropolitan hub, one of the most densely populated and economically significant.

cells: Haryana (west, north, south) and Uttar Pradesh (east, across the Yamuna) - only these two
Yamuna (flows through the eastern part of the city)
Delhi Ridge - a northern extension/outlier of the Aravalli Range, running through south, central and north Delhi
11 (as of the most recent reorganisation; earlier structured as 9)
Seat of the Government of India; New Delhi (within Delhi) is the formal capital
Core of the National Capital Region (NCR), which also includes parts of Haryana, UP and Rajasthan

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Don't confuse 'Delhi' (the full NCT, approx 1,484 sq km) with 'New Delhi' (a much smaller, planned area within Delhi that houses Parliament, Rashtrapati Bhavan and central government offices) or with 'NCR' (a much larger multi-state planning region including Gurugram, Noida, Faridabad, Ghaziabad etc.) - this three-way distinction is one of the most frequently tested geography-cum-polity points about Delhi.

The Delhi Ridge is a rocky quartzite outcrop, geologically the northernmost extension of the ancient Aravalli mountain range, entering Delhi from the south-west (near the Haryana border) and running in a broken, discontinuous line through South, Central and North Delhi before petering out near the Yamuna.

rows: Rocky outcrop acting as the northern tail of the Aravalli Range, providing ecological balance.
Low-lying alluvial plain along the eastern border, rich in agricultural sediment.

blocks.content: The Ridge is popularly called the 'green lungs of Delhi' because its forested stretches - including the Southern Ridge, Central Ridge (containing the historic Northern Ridge battle site of 1857), and the more recently created biodiversity parks - provide the city's most significant tracts of natural forest cover amid heavy urbanisation.

Because of its ecological importance, large parts of the Ridge are protected as Reserved Forest, and encroachment or diversion of Ridge land for construction remains a recurring subject of litigation and public debate.

★ EXAM POINT: 'Green lungs of Delhi' = the Delhi Ridge. Do not confuse this with the separate 'Yamuna Biodiversity Park' and other riverine green spaces, which are distinct, floodplain-based ecological zones rather than part of the rocky Ridge system.

items: The Delhi Ridge is a frequently tested topic—remember that it is an extension of the Aravalli Range.
Note that the Yamuna River defines the eastern boundary between Delhi and Uttar Pradesh.
Questions often cover the physical sub-regions of Delhi: the Ridge, the Yamuna floodplains, and the plains.

cells: Hot and dry; peak temperatures can exceed 45C, with occasional dust storms ('andhi') and heatwaves
South-West monsoon brings the bulk of annual rainfall, often causing urban waterlogging
Transitional; the onset of declining air quality due to stubble-burning in neighbouring states and reduced wind speeds
Cold, foggy; severe smog and hazardous Air Quality Index (AQI) episodes are a defining and heavily reported feature of Delhi winters

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Delhi's winter smog crisis - driven by a combination of vehicular/industrial emissions, dust, and seasonal crop-residue (stubble) burning in Punjab and Haryana - is one of the most consistently tested current-affairs-cum-environment topics for this UT (see Chapter 9).

items: Delhi (NCT): approx 1,484 sq km; borders only Haryana and Uttar Pradesh; sits on the Yamuna's west bank.
Delhi Ridge = northernmost extension of the Aravalli Range; called the 'green lungs of Delhi'.
Distinguish: Delhi (NCT, whole UT) is not New Delhi (small planned capital area within Delhi) is not NCR (larger multi-state region including Gurugram, Noida, Faridabad, Ghaziabad).
Delhi's winters are marked by severe smog/AQI crises, linked partly to stubble burning in neighbouring states.
